lead: Virtual memory separates the logical address space a process uses from the physical memory installed. With paging, the OS keeps only the pages a process touches in RAM and leaves the rest on disk. Demand paging loads a page on its first reference, so a large program starts quickly and can be larger than RAM. A laptop with many tabs and a phone opening apps both rely on this. The cost is the page fault, a trap that must be handled fast.
prereq: You need: 4.4 for pages and frames, 4.5 for page-table entries, and 4.2 for disk transfer.

blocks.text: Virtual memory is the separation of the logical address space from physical memory. A process gets a logical address space, independent of how much RAM is installed. With paging, this space is cut into pages and RAM into frames. The page table maps each page to a frame. Virtual memory lets the OS keep only the pages in use in frames and hold the rest in a swap area on disk. A program can then be larger than physical memory, and it can start before all its pages are loaded.

Demand paging loads a page only when it is referenced. The OS acts as a pager, also called a lazy swapper: it does not swap whole processes, it brings in pages. In the page-table entry (PTE), a valid bit records whether the page is in memory. Valid 1 means the frame number is usable. Valid 0 means the page is not in memory; touching it causes a trap. In a pure demand paging system, a process starts with no pages in memory. The first instruction immediately faults, then the working pages arrive one by one.

sections.h3: The page fault and its cost

blocks.text: A page fault is a trap caused by a reference to a page whose valid bit is 0. It is normal, not a program error. The hardware raises the trap; the OS handles it in this order:

items: Check the reference. If the address is outside the process's logical space, terminate with a segmentation fault. If legal but absent, continue.
Find a free frame, usually from a free-frame list. If none is free, choose a victim page (see 4.8).
If the victim page is dirty, write it back to its backing store: swap space for an anonymous page, or the mapped file for a file-backed page.
Set the victim's PTE valid bit to 0 and record where the victim page now lives: its swap slot or file location. The frame is now free for reuse.
Read the needed page from its backing store into the frame: swap space for an anonymous page, or the mapped file for a file-backed page.
Update the needed page's PTE: set valid 1 and write the frame number.
Restart the instruction that trapped. It now runs normally.

blocks.text: Let p be the page-fault rate, the fraction of memory references that fault. Let t<sub>a</sub> be memory access time and t<sub>s</sub> the page-fault service time. The effective access time is the average time per reference.

blocks.where: EAT is the effective access time per memory reference; p is the page-fault rate (0 ≤ p ≤ 1); t<sub>a</sub> is memory access time; t<sub>s</sub> is page-fault service time. Use the same unit for t<sub>a</sub> and t<sub>s</sub>.

blocks.text: The term (1 − p) × t<sub>a</sub> is the no-fault case. The term p × t<sub>s</sub> is the fault case. Because t<sub>s</sub> is measured in milliseconds and t<sub>a</sub> in nanoseconds, p must be tiny for EAT to stay close to t<sub>a</sub>.

After fork, parent and child usually have identical pages. Copying them all is wasteful. Copy-on-write (COW) makes both page tables point to the same frames, and marks each shared writable private page read-only as a copy-on-write page. When either process writes to such a page, the write-protection fault traps. The OS allocates a new frame, copies the page into it, marks the writer's PTE writable and points it to the new frame. The other process keeps the old page. A page that was already read-only, such as a code page, is not copied on a write: writing it remains a protection fault. Pages never written stay shared. When fork is followed by exec, COW saves most of the copy.
vfork is a special case: the child uses the parent's address space, and the parent is suspended until the child calls exec or exit. Do not let the child change memory under vfork.
Memory-mapped files use the same machinery: a file is mapped into the address space and its pages are faulted in on demand. File systems and mmap are in Unit 5.

spec.aria: A plot of effective access time in nanoseconds against page-fault rate in units of 10⁻⁶, with the line EAT = 200 + 7,999,800p rising from 200 ns at p = 0 to 240 ns at p = 5×10⁻⁶, a horizontal 220 ns limit line, and a marked point at p = 2.500062502×10⁻⁶ and EAT = 220 ns.

examples.question: A system has memory access time 200 ns and page-fault service time 8 ms. A slowdown of at most 10 percent is allowed. Find the largest page-fault rate p that keeps the effective access time within this limit, and the average number of references per page fault at that rate.
steps: Data: t<sub>a</sub> = 200 ns. t<sub>s</sub> = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns because 1 ms = 1,000,000 ns.
A 10 percent slowdown means EAT ≤ 1.10 × 200 = 220 ns.
examples.answer: The fault rate must satisfy p ≤ 2.500062502 × 10⁻⁶, about one fault in 399,990 references, and the allowed effective access time is 220 ns.
examples.check:
ma_ns = 200.0
fault_ns = 8_000_000.0
limit_ns = 1.10 * ma_ns
p_max = (limit_ns - ma_ns) / (fault_ns - ma_ns)
refs = 1.0 / p_max
print(f"{p_max:.10g}")
print(int(round(refs)))
print(round(limit_ns, 1))

traps: Dropping the (1 − p) factor and using EAT = p × t<sub>s</sub> only. The no-fault case still costs one memory access.
Mixing milliseconds and nanoseconds. Convert 8 ms to 8,000,000 ns before putting it into the formula.
Treating a page fault as an error. A legal page that is merely absent from memory causes a normal trap and is loaded on demand.
Using p as a percentage. p = 0.1 means 10 percent of references fault, not 0.1 percent.
Thinking COW copies every page at fork. COW copies a page only when one process first writes to it.

quiz.a: A page fault is a trap raised when a process references a page whose valid bit is 0, meaning the page is not currently in memory.

quiz.q: Why can a process be larger than physical memory under demand paging?
quiz.a: Only the pages currently referenced must be in frames. The remaining pages stay in swap space and are loaded when touched, so the logical address space can exceed RAM.

quiz.q: A system has t<sub>a</sub> = 100 ns, t<sub>s</sub> = 5 ms and p = 0.0001. Compute EAT in nanoseconds.
Why must p be tiny? Use the ratio t<sub>s</sub> ÷ t<sub>a</sub>.
quiz.a: The fault term is p × t<sub>s</sub>. If t<sub>s</sub> is 8,000,000 ns and t<sub>a</sub> is 200 ns, one fault adds the equivalent of 40,000 memory accesses. Even a small p then dominates EAT.

quiz.q: What does valid bit 0 mean? Is every such reference a program error?
quiz.a: It means the page is not in memory. It is not necessarily an error: if the address is legal, the OS loads the page and restarts the instruction. An address outside the logical space is the error case.

quiz.q: In copy-on-write after fork, when is a page actually copied?
quiz.a: Only when the parent or child writes to a shared page. The write-protection fault makes the OS copy that page into a new frame for the writer; unwritten pages remain shared.

quiz.q: What does vfork guarantee about the parent?
quiz.a: The parent is suspended until the child calls exec or exit, and the child uses the parent's address space.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linux reports minor faults, where the page is in memory but not mapped, and major faults, which need disk I/O. Huge pages reduce fault and TLB cost for large working sets. Containers use memory cgroups to limit resident pages, which changes fault behaviour under pressure. Search for demand paging, copy-on-write fork and minor vs major page fault.
